cards.question: Why was CS 8803 Graduate Introduction to Operating Systems created as a companion to the Advanced Operating Systems course (CS 6210)?
cards.answer: The graduate student population diversified over time, and many students arrived without formal OS training or hadn't reviewed OS basics in years, creating a gap that this introductory course addresses.

cards.question: What is the success metric the instructor gives for completing this course?
cards.answer: After finishing the course, a student should be able to answer every question on the diagnostic test associated with the Advanced Operating Systems (CS 6210) course.

cards.question: What are the three core learning goals of this course?
cards.answer: To understand what operating systems are, why they are needed, and how they are designed and implemented.

cards.question: What major OS topic areas does the course cover in depth?
cards.answer: Processes and process management; threads, concurrency, and multithreading challenges; OS management of hardware resources (CPU, memory); OS communication and I/O services (including file I/O); and OS support for distributed services such as remote procedure calls (RPCs), distributed file systems, and distributed shared memory.

cards.question: Why does the course include a practical (programming) component alongside the theoretical material?
cards.answer: To fully understand and appreciate OS internals, hands-on programming projects give students direct experience with challenges like multithreading, concurrency, synchronization, inter-process communication, and building distributed/multi-node services using OS-level mechanisms like RPC.

cards.question: What programming language and environment are used for the course's programming projects, and what threading library is required?
cards.answer: Projects are written in C on a Linux environment, using standard Linux libraries such as Pthreads for multithreading.

cards.question: Besides functional correctness, what other kind of skill do the programming projects aim to build?
cards.answer: Experience designing and performing experimental performance evaluations, to gain insight into an OS's behavior, performance capabilities, overheads, and limitations.

cards.question: What is the recommended (though not required) textbook situation for this course?
cards.answer: There is no required textbook, but a solid OS textbook is recommended as reference — examples given include Silberschatz's 'Operating System Concepts' (the 'dinosaur book'), Tanenbaum's 'Modern Operating Systems', and the free online book 'Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces' by Arpaci-Dusseau.

cards.question: How is the course grade broken down?
cards.answer: Midterm exam 25%, final exam 30% (not cumulative), programming projects 40%, and class participation 5%.

cards.question: What counts toward the class participation portion of the grade?
cards.answer: Participation in the Piazza online forum (answering others' questions, raising useful discussion topics) and performance on quizzes embedded in the Audacity platform lessons.

cards.question: What are the exam policies for this course?
cards.answer: Exams are proctored online via a service called ProctorU, taken individually, and are closed-notes, closed-book.

cards.question: What are the collaboration rules for programming projects?
cards.answer: Students may work in teams and can have high-level cross-team discussions about design or implementation approach, but may not share code, results, or final report text; such discussions should happen through Piazza so staff and other students can help.

cards.question: What visual/toy-shop metaphor does the instructor use throughout the course to explain OS concepts, and what does each part represent?
cards.answer: The computer hardware is represented as a toy shop (with its tools, workspaces, and storage areas); the processes/applications running on the hardware are the toys being produced; and the operating system is represented as the toy shop manager overseeing everything happening in the shop.
